headline: Chinese AI models offer GPT-4o performance for 97% less money after two weeks of testing
summary: A developer tested DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, finding some deliver GPT-4o level results for a fraction of the cost. One model processes a million tokens for just one cent.
details: A developer, initially defaulting to GPT-4o, was surprised by the capabilities and cost-effectiveness of Chinese AI models after two weeks of testing. They discovered several models that could perform similarly to GPT-4o for significantly less money, challenging their prior assumptions about the AI landscape.

The testing focused on four major Chinese AI families: DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, each with multiple versions and varying price points. Key findings included DeepSeek V4 Flash as a budget-friendly winner, Qwen for its wide range of model options, Kimi for strong reasoning, and GLM for excelling in Chinese language tasks.

DeepSeek V4 Flash emerged as a standout, costing just $0.25 per million tokens, a fraction of GPT-4o prices. The developer found it capable of handling tasks they previously used GPT-4o for, including coding problems, content writing, and brainstorming.

Its code generation was particularly impressive, consistently delivering top-tier output and ranking high on the HumanEval benchmark for its price range. DeepSeek also offers a dedicated Coder model at the same price, and the V4 Flash model achieved speeds of around 60 tokens per second.

However, DeepSeek has some limitations, including weaker vision capabilities and slightly less proficient Chinese language skills compared to GLM and Kimi. It also offers fewer model size options than Qwen, which provides a broader selection.

Qwen, developed by Alibaba, was described as the 'Swiss Army knife' of Chinese AI due to its extensive range of models for various needs. Its pricing structure is remarkably diverse, ranging from $0.01 to $3.20 per million tokens within the same family.

The Qwen3-32B model, priced at $0.28 per million tokens, was a favorite for its balance of affordability and intelligence, performing well in general coding and content creation. The developer noted that Qwen's extensive model naming conventions could be confusing for new users.

headline_marked: [[OpenAI Assistants API shuts off]] August 26, 2026, requiring manual migration.
headline: OpenAI Assistants API shuts off August 26, 2026, requiring manual migration.
summary: OpenAI is discontinuing its Assistants API on August 26, 2026. Developers must manually migrate their applications as there will be no grace period, degraded mode, or migration tool from OpenAI.
details: OpenAI is officially shutting down its Assistants API on August 26, 2026. After this date, endpoints like /v1/assistants, /v1/threads, and /v1/threads/runs will return errors without a grace period or degraded mode. OpenAI has confirmed it will not provide a migration tool, making a manual transition essential for developers.

The migration involves moving to the new Responses API and Conversations. A key change is the shift from asynchronous Run objects, which required polling, to synchronous Response calls that provide immediate results. This eliminates the need for polling loops in your code.

For Python and JS/TS SDKs, client.beta.threads.runs.create(...) becomes client.responses.create(...), and client.beta.threads.create() transitions to client.conversations.create(). To maintain multi-turn history, developers will create a Conversation and pass its ID instead of rebuilding threads.

Beyond simple renames, developers face three significant changes: existing Threads will not auto-migrate to Conversations, requiring manual replay or dropping of history. Assistant configuration moves from code to a versioned Prompt object, altering how config is stored. Tool wiring also changes, with tool calls and outputs becoming Items in the response stream instead of steps on a Run.

Given the manual nature of the rewrite, an exact inventory of beta.assistants and beta.threads call sites is crucial. Implementing CI gates to fail builds if old call sites reappear post-migration can prevent regressions. An open-source scanner, openai-assistants-sunset, is available to assist with inventory and CI checks.
